summary: Describes the set of Microsoft vendor-specific RADIUS attributes, which carry extra information between network access servers and authentication servers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2548 lists extra RADIUS attributes used by Microsoft dial-up protocols and products. It explains how those attributes are packed and what information they carry.

questions: what are microsoft vendor specific radius attributes
subtitle: A reference to Microsoft-specific attributes carried inside RADIUS packets.

tldr.problem: The standard RADIUS attributes did not cover some Microsoft dial-up protocols and features, making an open description useful to other implementers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines Microsoft sub-attributes carried in a Vendor-Specific RADIUS attribute whose Vendor-ID is 311. They cover authentication, encryption keys, bandwidth allocation, ARAP, and other settings.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2548 is Informational, not a standard. It was intended as an open reference and expected to be updated when Microsoft defined new attributes.

today: RFC 2548 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document describes these attributes as a reference for interoperability, not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why Microsoft RADIUS Attributes Exist
sections.content:
The memo describes Microsoft vendor-specific RADIUS attributes. They support Microsoft proprietary dial-up protocols or features not supplied by the standard RADIUS attribute set.

Its stated purpose is to provide an open, accessible reference for third parties that want to interoperate with Microsoft products. The memo says it does not specify an Internet standard and was expected to be updated when new Microsoft attributes were defined.
sections.plainLanguage: These attributes add information used by Microsoft dial-up features to RADIUS packets. The memo documents them so other implementations can interoperate.

sections.title: Carrying Vendor-Specific Sub-attributes
sections.content:
Each Microsoft sub-attribute is carried inside a RADIUS Vendor-Specific attribute. Its Vendor-ID must be decimal 311. A single outer attribute may contain multiple sub-attributes, each encoded as Vendor-Type, Vendor-Length, and Value.

When several sub-attributes share one outer attribute, its Length must equal the sum of their Vendor-Length values plus six. The memo also provides a table showing which sub-attributes may appear in different RADIUS packet types.
sections.plainLanguage: A RADIUS Vendor-Specific attribute contains Microsoft's Vendor-ID and one or more sub-attributes. Each sub-attribute includes a type, length, and value.

sections.title: MS-CHAP Authentication Attributes
sections.content:
The memo defines attributes for MS-CHAP version 1 and version 2. Version 1 includes a challenge and a response containing separate LM and NT response fields; the MS-CHAP-Response attribute has Vendor-Length 52, and each response field is 24 octets.

Version 2 adds mutual authentication. Its response includes a 16-octet Peer-Challenge and a 24-octet Response. A separate success attribute carries a 42-octet authenticator response string. Other attributes support password changes and error information.
sections.plainLanguage: MS-CHAP attributes carry challenges and responses used to check a login. Version 2 also carries a peer challenge and a server response for mutual authentication.

sections.title: MPPE Keys and Encryption Settings
sections.content:
Microsoft Point-to-Point Encryption (MPPE) encrypts PPP packets with RC4 and supports 40-bit and 128-bit session keys. The memo defines attributes for MPPE keys and for indicating whether encryption is allowed or required.

Send and receive key attributes include a two-octet Salt that must have its leftmost bit set and must be unique within the packet. The key string is padded to a multiple of 16 octets and encrypted using the shared secret, the Request Authenticator, and the Salt.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS can carry MPPE keys and settings for PPP encryption. The key attributes use a Salt and a specified method to protect the key while it is carried.

sections.title: Bandwidth, ARAP, and Other Attributes
sections.content:
Bandwidth Allocation Protocol attributes say whether BAP is allowed or required, set a link-utilization threshold, and specify how long a link must stay below that threshold before it is dropped. The threshold value is from 1 through 100.

Other attributes support Apple Remote Access Protocol (ARAP), identify the RADIUS client and software version, carry traffic filters, record authentication type, and provide primary or secondary DNS and NetBIOS name-server addresses for a PPP peer.
sections.plainLanguage: Other sub-attributes carry settings for link bandwidth, ARAP passwords, traffic filters, accounting, and name-server addresses. The BAP threshold controls when an underused link may be dropped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says MS-CHAP is susceptible to dictionary attacks, so users should choose passwords carefully and make them long enough to deter easy guessing.

RADIUS proxies decrypt and re-encrypt the protected MPPE key fields when forwarding them. The memo therefore says those attributes should not be used on networks with untrusted RADIUS proxies.
sections.plainLanguage: Weak passwords can be guessed, so the memo recommends passwords long enough to deter easy guessing. Key attributes pass through proxies that decrypt and re-encrypt them.
